question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=x^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=\left(x + 7\right)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=2 x,\quad v'(x)=2 x + 14.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(2 x)(\left(x + 7\right)^{2})-(x^{2})(2 x + 14)}{(\left(x + 7\right)^{2})^2} \\ & =\frac{14 x}{\left(x + 7\right)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: All real x where the displayed denominator is nonzero.

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\tan{\left(x \right)}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2 x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1,\quad v'(x)=2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1)(2 x)-(\tan{\left(x \right)})(2)}{(2 x)^2} \\ & =\frac{x \tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + x - \tan{\left(x \right)}}{2 x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=(x+1)^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)={x}^{2}+1.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=2(x+1),\,{v}^{′}(x)=2x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2(x+1))({x}^{2}+1)-((x+1)^{2})(2x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)-2x(x+1)^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)(({x}^{2}+1)-x(x+1))}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)({x}^{2}+1-{x}^{2}-x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(x+1)(1-x)}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-{x}^{2})}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u'(x)=- \sin{\left(x \right)},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(- \sin{\left(x \right)})(x)-(\cos{\left(x \right)})(1)}{(x)^2} \\ & =- \frac{x \sin{\left(x \right)} + \cos{\left(x \right)}}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value at $x=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{2}{3 \pi} \\ & =\frac{2}{3 \pi}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=e^{x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=e^{x},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(e^{x})(x)-(e^{x})(1)}{(x)^2} \\ & =\frac{\left(x - 1\right) e^{x}}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y'(1) & =0 \\ & =0.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(t)=t$ and the denominator $v(t)=\left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating $u(t)$ and $v(t),$ we have

$$
u'(t)=1,\quad v'(t)=4 t \left(t^{2} + 1\right).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{u'(t)v(t)-u(t)v'(t)}{[v(t)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(1)(\left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{2})-(t)(4 t \left(t^{2} + 1\right))}{(\left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{2})^2} \\ & =- \frac{3 t^{2} - 1}{\left(t^{2} + 1\right)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$
